# Chapter 5: Results

\noindent\hrulefill

## 5.1 Descriptive Statistics

```{r tab-summary-stats}
datasummary_df(
  summ_table,
  title = 'Summary Statistics',
  fmt = 2,
  output = 'kableExtra'
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = 'HOLD_position')  # strong hold
```

```{r tab-summary-stats-win}
datasummary_df(
  summ_table_w,
  title = 'Summary Statistics (Post-Winsorization)',
  fmt = 2,
  output = 'kableExtra'
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = 'HOLD_position')  # strong hold
```

Tables 2 and 3 present the summary statistics of the key variables used in our analysis. Table 2 reports the baseline statistics, while Table 3 reports the statistics after winsorizing the credit variables (liquidity and leverage) at the 1st and 99th percentiles to mitigate the influence of extreme outliers.

The GVC position index ($gvc\_position$) is unbounded in theory, but in practice is constrained by the underlying distribution of forward and backward participation. In our data, the measure is skewed toward negative values, reflecting the predominance of downstream, import-intensive firms. It has a mean close to zero (0.04) with a relatively small standard deviation (0.20), indicating that most firms are clustered around the middle of the value chain rather than at either extreme end of the production chain.

Among the explanatory variables, firm productivity ($lag\_tfp$) shows substantial variation with a range of -9.51 to 1.82, reflecting heterogeneity in firm efficiency. Firm size and age also display considerable variation, reflecting a mix of young and older, established firms.

The credit variables in Table 2 show extreme ranges and very high standard deviations: liquidity ($lag\_liq$) has a standard deviation of 33.33 while for leverage ($lag\_lev$) it is 11.31 with maximum values far exceeding typical firm-level values, suggesting the presence of significant outliers. To address this issue, both variables are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles in Table 3. Post-winsorization, the distributions become much more stable: the standard deviations of both liquidity and leverage decline (from 33.33 to 0.48 for liquidity; from 11.31 to 0.31 for leverage), with corresponding reductions in their minimum and maximum values respectively. We use these winsorized variables in our regression models.

Finally, capability-related variables such as advertising intensity ($lag\_adv$) and innovation ($lag\_innov$) are concentrated at relatively low values with low standard deviation, indicating that most firms engage only minimally in these activities. Since investments in branding and innovation are concentrated among only a small subset of firms, it may imply that only a few firms possess the market-facing and knowledge-based capabilities required to move toward higher value-added segments of the value chain. In contrast, ICT intensity ($lag_ict$) exhibits a relatively higher mean and smaller dispersion, suggesting more consistent engagement across firms. This indicates that basic digital or ICT-related expenditures are more widespread compared to innovation and advertising.

```{r fig-corrplot, out.width='100%', fig.cap="Correlation Matrix", fig.pos='H'}
knitr::include_graphics('F:/r/thesis-gvc-position/output/images/corrplot.png')
```

Figure 1 shows the correlation matrix of our key variables and indicates that pairwise correlations among them are generally low, suggesting the absence of strong linear relationships. Most coefficients are close to zero, with the exception of a moderate negative correlation between leverage and liquidity. The relatively weak correlations imply that multicollinearity is unlikely to be a major concern in the regression analysis. At the same time, the low correlation between capability variables (innovation, advertising and ICT) and GVC position suggests that their effects may not operate in isolation but rather through more complex, interactive channels. Further, these relationships may be obscured by significant firm-level heterogeneity, which cannot be captured in simple pairwise correlations and instead necessitates a fixed-effects framework. This motivates the inclusion of interaction terms and firm-level controls in the empirical specification.

```{r fig-firm-count, out.width='100%', fig.cap="Distribution of Firms Across Industries", fig.pos='H'}
knitr::include_graphics('F:/r/thesis-gvc-position/output/images/firm-count-distribution.png')
```

The distribution of firms across industries in the sample is highly uneven, with a few sectors accounting for a disproportionately large share of observations (Figure 2). ISIC code 32 (other manufacturing, including jewellery, musical instruments, medical instruments etc) has the largest representation with 2,187 firms, followed by chemicals (20: 1,809), electrical equipment (27: 1,506) and textiles (13: 1,157). Other relatively well-represented sectors include food products (10: 1,143), machinery (28: 954) and motor vehicles (29: 934). Since the measure of forward GVC participation in our research relies on industry-level proxies, we disaggregate industry 24 (basic metals) and industry 30 (transport equipment) into their constituent sub-sectors following the OECD classification. Some of these sub-sectors notably have the least number of firms: 303 (8 firms), 301 (14 firms), 2432 (24 firms) and 302 (40 firms), alongside sector 31 (furniture, with 24 firms). Since the sample remains concentrated in a few key manufacturing sectors, our empirical estimation strategy must address this industry-level heterogeneity.

## 5.2 The Impact of Productivity on GVC Upgrading

Table 4 estimates our first hypothesis relating firm productivity to GVC positioning under the three alternate specifications: (1) industry and year fixed effects, (2) industry-year fixed effects, and (3) firm fixed effects. Total factor productivity $(lag\_tfp)$ emerges as the most robust determinant of GVC position, with a positive and highly significant coefficient across all three models. Thus, both cross-sectional and within-firm improvements in productivity can improve GVC positioning, confirming earlier studies that found productivity to be a key driver of moving up within GVCs. In fact, a 1% increase in (lagged) TFP raises relative firm position within the value chain by 0.11 to 0.21 units, either by reducing import dependence (holding forward contribution constant), or increasing value-added of intermediate exports (holding import intensity constant), or both. 

```{r tab-productivity, results='asis'}

models_prod <- list(
  'Industry & Year FE' = prod1,
  'Industry-Year FE'   = prod2,
  'Firm FE'            = prod3
)

modelsummary(models_prod,
             output = 'kableExtra',
             title = 'Panel Regression for Firm Productivity',
             stars = TRUE,
             fmt = 3,                     # decimal rounding
             add_rows = fe_rows,          # fixed effects
             gof_map = fitstats) %>%      # fitstats
  kable_styling(latex_options = 'HOLD_position')

```

Firm age is statistically significant and positively associated with GVC position, implying that older established firms are positioned farther up the production chain than newer firms. They also tend to rely less on imported inputs and export more value in the form of more sophisticated intermediate. 

The most interesting result is the coefficient on size $(size\_new)$, which is negative. Generally, we expect larger firms to be positioned higher in the value chain since they have the capacity for R&D and brand-building to improve product quality and differentiate their product from competitors. But our results imply that larger firms (here, firms with a larger asset base) may be more assembly-oriented with higher import dependence instead of high value-added exporters. Reddy and Sasidharan (2021) find that larger firms tend to *participate* more in GVCs, but out findings suggest that such firms are more likely to operate in low value-added segments of the production chain, becoming trapped in the "captive effect" that Thakur and Sharma (2025) warn about.

Within $R^2$ is low across all specifications. A comparatively higher Adjusted $R^2$ reveals that the models mainly capture between-firm differences as opposed to within-firm variations, indicating the low explanatory power of our productivity model.

Overall, however, higher productivity is associated with better GVC positioning. Firms that improve their productivity are able to move further up in the value chain over time (i.e. upgrade) as shown by the statistically significant coefficient on $lag\_tfp$ in the firm FE specification. TFP has a robust and consistent effect across all specifications, though the magnitude is modest, reflecting the gradual nature of upgrading within GVCs.

## 5.3 The Impact of Credit Constraints on GVC Upgrading

### 5.3.1 The Liquidity Mechanism

Table 5 estimates our second hypothesis relating firm productivity to GVC positioning under the three alternate specifications: (1) industry and year fixed effects, (2) industry-year fixed effects, and (3) firm fixed effects. Access to working capital $(lag\_liq\_w)$ does not emerge as a statistically significant determinant of GVC position across any of the specifications. This suggests that short-term liquidity constraints do not play a decisive role in shaping a firm’s position within the value chain *in isolation*. In other words, simply having greater access to working capital does not necessarily enable firms to reduce import dependence or increase the domestic value-added content of their exports. This contrasts with the findings of Manova and Yu (2016) who found liquidity to be a significant driver of upgrading for Chinese firms, though they do not include an interaction term in their model.

The lack of significance across all three specifications also indicates that neither cross-sectional differences and within-firm changes in liquidity are associated with GVC upgrading. While access to finance is often viewed as a critical enabler of firm performance, these results imply that liquidity primarily supports routine operational activities rather than strategic upgrading into higher value-added segments of production. This is consistent with the idea that financial resources alone are insufficient without complementary firm capabilities, such as productivity, innovation or market power.

```{r tab-credit-liquidity, results='asis'}

models_liq <- list(
  'Industry & Year FE' = liq1,
  'Industry-Year FE'   = liq2,
  'Firm FE'            = liq3
)

modelsummary(models_liq,
             output = 'kableExtra',
             title = 'Panel Regression for Working Capital Access',
             stars = TRUE,
             fmt = 3,                     # decimal rounding
             add_rows = fe_rows,          # fixed effects
             gof_map = fitstats) %>%      # fitstats
  kable_styling(latex_options = 'HOLD_position')

```

Moreover, the coefficient on liquidity declines in magnitude when moving to the firm fixed effects specification, reinforcing the interpretation that earlier variation is likely driven by time-invariant firm characteristics such as managerial quality, established banking relationships or network advantages rather than a causal effect of liquidity itself. Even though Reddy and Sasidharan (2021) find working capital access to be a significant driver of GVC *participation* of Indian firms, our results suggest that the role of liquidity may end there.

The interaction term between liquidity and productivity $(lag\_liq\_w \cdot lag\_tfp)$ provides limited evidence of complementarity between financial access and firm capabilities. In the first specification, the coefficient is positive and weakly significant, suggesting that firms with both higher productivity and better working capital access may be better able to upgrade. However, this effect does not persist in the firm fixed effects specification, where the interaction term becomes insignificant. This indicates that the observed complementarity is not robust to controlling for unobserved, time-invariant firm characteristics and likely reflects structural differences across firms—such as managerial quality, established banking relationships or network advantages rather than a causal mechanism where access to working capital enhances the impact of productivity on GVC positioning.

Within $R^2$ is low across all specifications (~4%; drops to 0.9% in the firm FE specification). A comparatively higher Adjusted $R^2$ reveals that the model mainly captures between-firm differences rather than within-firm variation, indicating the limited explanatory power of working capital access in driving changes in GVC positioning.

Figure 3 estimates industry-specific estimates of liquidity on GVC position, revealing substantial heterogeneity in the relation. While certain sectors such as printing (ISIC 18), non-metallic minerals (23) and fabricated metals (2431, 2432) exhibit a strong and positive association, several core manufacturing industries including machinery (28), automobiles (29), furniture (31) and other manufacturing (32) show a negative and statistically significant relationship. Wide confidence intervals observed in smaller industries (e.g. ISIC 301, 302) indicating low precision due to limited firm representation. These results highlight that the role of working capital in facilitating upgrading is highly context-specific and mediated by industry structure, rather than being universally beneficial.

```{r fig-indspecific-liq, out.width='100%', fig.cap="Industry-Specific Effect of Liquidity on GVC position", fig.pos='H'}
knitr::include_graphics('F:/r/thesis-gvc-position/output/images/industry-beta-liq.png')
```

Overall, the findings suggest that while working capital may be necessary for sustained GVC participation (Reddy & Sasidharan, 2021), it is not a binding constraint for moving up the value chain. Instead, upgrading appears to depend more critically on deeper structural capabilities, with liquidity playing at most a supportive but not transformative role. This is further reinforced by our industry-specific results, which reveal substantial heterogeneity in the relation between liquidity and GVC position. While liquidity facilitates upgrading in certain sectors, in others it is either insignificant or even negatively associated with GVC position, suggesting that additional financial resources may be directed toward expanding existing production rather than functional upgrading.

### 5.3.2 The Leverage Mechanism

Table 6 again estimates our second hypothesis relating firm productivity to GVC positioning under the three alternate specifications: (1) industry and year fixed effects, (2) industry-year fixed effects, and (3) firm fixed effects. Firm debt burden $(lag\_lev\_w)$ has a negative and statistically significant association with GVC position, though this effect disappears once firm fixed effects are introduced. In particular, the coefficients in the first two models suggest that a 1% increase in lagged leverage reduces a firm’s GVC position by ~0.13 units, indicating that more indebted firms are located lower in the value chain. This may reflect greater reliance on imported inputs or a lower capacity to generate domestic value-added through exports, supporting Manova and Yu (2016) who similarly find leverage to be a statistically significant constraint on GVC upgrading, though their estimated effect is smaller (0.002-0.005). However, importantly, the coefficient becomes insignificant in the firm fixed effects specification implying that this relationship is largely driven by cross-sectional differences rather than within-firm changes over time.

The results therefore suggest that highly leveraged firms are structurally disadvantaged in terms of GVC positioning, possibly due to financial constraints that limit their ability to invest in upgrading activities such as innovation, quality improvement or branding. At the same time, the absence of a significant within-firm effect indicates that fluctuations in debt levels do not impede within-firm upgrading.

The interaction term between leverage and productivity $(lag\_lev\_w \cdot lag\_tfp)$ is negative and significant in the first two specifications, suggesting that higher debt burdens dampen the positive effect of productivity on GVC positioning. In other words, even productive firms may be unable to translate efficiency gains into upgrading when constrained by high leverage. However, similar to the main effect, this interaction becomes insignificant under firm fixed effects, i.e., it is not robust to unobserved firm heterogeneity.

Within $R^2$ is low across all specifications (~4%; drops to 1.5% in the firm FE specification). A comparatively higher Adjusted $R^2$ suggests that the model primarily captures cross-sectional differences across firms rather than within-firm variation, indicating the limited role firm leverage in explaining GVC upgrading over time.

```{r tab-credit-leverage, results='asis'}

models_lev <- list(
  'Industry & Year FE' = lev1,
  'Industry-Year FE'   = lev2,
  'Firm FE'            = lev3
)

modelsummary(models_lev,
             output = 'kableExtra',
             title = 'Panel Regression for Firm Debt Burden',
             stars = TRUE,
             fmt = 3,                     # decimal rounding
             add_rows = fe_rows,          # fixed effects
             gof_map = fitstats) %>%      # fitstats
  kable_styling(latex_options = 'HOLD_position')

```

The industry-specific estimates for leverage reveal a more consistent pattern compared to liquidity (Figure 4), with a majority of core manufacturing sectors exhibiting a negative and statistically significant relationship between leverage and GVC position, confirming our previous regression results. Industries such as food processing (10), petroleum products (19), metals (27), machinery (28), automobiles (29) and other manufacturing (32) show that higher debt burdens are associated with a decline in GVC position. This suggests that external financing, unlike internal liquidity, may constrain firms’ ability to upgrade. While a few sectors such as printing (18), non-metallic minerals (23) and certain metal sub-sectors (2431, 2432) display positive effects, these are exceptions and in some cases accompanied by wide confidence intervals, indicating lower precision. Thus, our results highlight that leverage may reinforce firms’ engagement in lower value-added activities rather than facilitating movement toward higher value-added segments, particularly in scale-intensive manufacturing.

```{r fig-indspecific-lev, out.width='100%', fig.cap="Industry-Specific Effect of Leverage on GVC position", fig.pos='H'}
knitr::include_graphics('F:/r/thesis-gvc-position/output/images/industry-beta-lev.png')
```

Overall, the findings point to a nuanced role of financial structure in shaping GVC outcomes. While higher leverage is associated with poorer GVC positioning in cross-sectional estimates, its within-firm effect suggests that debt does not uniformly impede upgrading over time. Instead, the impact of leverage varies across industries. In several core manufacturing sectors such as machinery, automobiles and machinery, higher leverage is associated with a decline in GVC position. In contrast, certain industries exhibit a positive relationship, suggesting that external financing may facilitate movement into higher value-added functions where capital requirements are substantial. At the same time, wide confidence intervals in smaller industries point to limited precision in our estimates. Overall, conditional on firm productivity, higher leverage is associated with lower GVC positioning in the cross-section, but it does not necessarily drive within-firm upgrading, and the effect varies by industry-specific contexts.

## 5.4 The Impact of Firm-Capabilities on GVC Upgrading

Firm capabilities, proxied by advertising intensity $(lag\_adv)$ and innovation $(lag\_innov)$, emerge as important determinants of GVC position, though their robustness and persistence vary (Table 7). The coefficient on advertising is strongly positive and significant across all three specifications, including under firm FE. In fact, a 1% increase in advertising is associated with a 0.19 unit rise in GVC position. This suggests that both cross-sectional differences and within-firm increases in branding, marketing and distribution enable firms to move toward higher value-added segments of the value chain. Higher advertising intensity likely reflects stronger brand-building and market-facing capabilities, which allow firms to differentiate their products, command higher margins (market power) and reduce dependence on low-value assembly activities. This is consistent with Arneja and Sharma (2024) who similarly find advertising investments to enable higher value capture, although our coefficients are notably larger.

In contrast, innovation $(lag\_innov)$ shows a positive and significant effect only in the first two specifications, with coefficients of 0.125 and 0.116 in models (1) and (2) respectively. However, this effect becomes insignificant in the firm fixed effects specification. This indicates that while more innovative firms tend to be positioned higher in the value chain (cross-sectional difference), within-firm increases in innovation do not translate into upgrading over time. One possible explanation is that the observed cross-sectional relationship may capture persistent firm characteristics like technological capability or R&D orientation rather than a direct causal effect. Secondly, R&D intensity might itself be a weak proxy for innovation. Both Choi et al. (2019) and Thakur and Sharma (2025) find a positive, statistically significant link between GVC position and innovation at the country and industry levels respectively; but they also proxy innovation using the number of patent applications.

```{r tab-capabilities, results='asis'}

models_capab <- list(
  'Industry & Year FE' = capab1,
  'Industry-Year FE'   = capab2,
  'Firm FE'            = capab3
)

modelsummary(models_capab,
             output = 'kableExtra',
             title = 'Panel Regression for Firm Capabilities',
             stars = TRUE,
             fmt = 3,                     # decimal rounding
             add_rows = fe_rows,          # fixed effects
             gof_map = fitstats) %>%      # fitstats
  kable_styling(latex_options = 'HOLD_position')

```

Within $R^2$ is low across all specifications (~12-13%; plunges to 2% in the firm FE specification), though relatively higher than in the financial models. A comparatively higher Adjusted $R^2$ (34-39%; rises to 85% in the final specification) indicates that the model still largely captures between-firm differences rather than within-firm variation, suggesting that firm capabilities are more important in explaining cross-sectional differences than short-run changes in GVC positioning.

These results highlight an important distinction between different types of firm capabilities. While both advertising and innovation are associated with improved GVC positioning, only advertising demonstrates a robust within-firm effect, suggesting that market-facing capabilities play a more consistent role in enabling upgrading within GVCs. Innovation, on the other hand, appears to explain structural differences in the cross-section rather than a driver of movement along the value chain.

### 5.4.1. The Role of Information & Communication Technology

To examine the role of digital technologies in an increasingly interconnected global economy, we estimate two firm fixed-effects models: one focusing on advertising and the other on innovation. In each specification, we interact the respective capability variable with ICT intensity to assess whether digital capabilities complement these firm-level investments in driving GVC upgrading.

```{r tab-ICT-adv, results='asis'}

modelsummary(ict_adv,
             output = 'kableExtra',
             title = 'Panel Regression for Advertising × ICT',
             col.names = NULL,
             stars = TRUE,
             fmt = 3,                     # decimal rounding
             gof_map = fitstats) %>%      # fitstats
  kable_styling(latex_options = 'HOLD_position')

```

Table 8 shows the how advertising interacts with ICT usage. The interaction between advertising intensity ($lag\_advert$) and ICT ($lag\_ict$) has a positive and statistically significant effect on GVC position, highlighting a strong complementarity between market-facing and digital capabilities. While advertising intensity alone shows a weak negative association with GVC upgrading, and ICT intensity by itself remains insignificant, their combined effect is positive, suggesting that digital capability enhances the effectiveness of advertising in enabling firms to move toward higher value-added segments. This supports Oh and Hwang (2025) in their view that digital capabilities can act as "VRIN" resources, providing sustained comparative advantages and enable upgrading. Investments in branding and market expansion translate into upgrading only when supported by adequate ICT infrastructure, which facilitates market access, coordination and customer engagement. This is in line with Linbing et al. (2023)'s findings that the firm’s ability to internalize and innovate is what drives value capture, rather than simply participating in such functions.

```{r tab-ICT-innov, results='asis'}

modelsummary(ict_innov,
             output = 'kableExtra',
             title = 'Panel Regression for Innovation × ICT',
             col.names = NULL,
             stars = TRUE,
             fmt = 3,                     # decimal rounding
             gof_map = fitstats) %>%      # fitstats
  kable_styling(latex_options = 'HOLD_position')

```

In contrast to the advertising, neither innovation nor its interaction with ICT exhibits a statistically significant effect on GVC position (Table 9). The coefficients on innovation ($lag\_innov$), ICT intensity ($lag\_ict$) and their interaction are all insignificant, suggesting that investments in innovation do not translate into observable upgrading within the value chain (at least in the short run). This may reflect the long gestation period of R&D activities, where gains in product sophistication materialize only over a longer horizon. Additionally, the relatively smaller sample size and limited within-firm variation in innovation expenditure may further reduce the ability to detect significant effects in a fixed-effects framework. Our results do not find strong support for Oh and Hwang (2025)'s claims on digital capabilities enhancing innovation and promoting functional upgrading, although we do find support for the advertising channel.

The results point to a conditional role of digital capability in driving GVC upgrading: ICT intensity on its own does not have a significant effect, but plays a complementary role when combined with market-facing capabilities such as advertising. In contrast, no such complementarity is observed with innovation, suggesting that the interaction between digital capability and R&D is less immediate and may operate over longer time horizons. Overall, these findings indicate that digital technologies are not independently sufficient for upgrading, but act as an enabling infrastructure that amplifies specific firm capabilities, particularly those linked to market access.

## 5.5 Diagnostics Tests

### 5.5.1 Hausman Test

```{r tab-hausman}

datasummary_df(
  hausman_table,
  title = 'Results of Hausman Test',
  output = 'kableExtra',
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = 'HOLD_position')

```

The Hausman test results (Table 10) indicate that while the productivity (baseline) specification does not show significant differences between fixed and random effects, the inclusion of financial and capability-related variables leads to systematic rejection of the random effects model. This suggests that key explanatory variables such as liquidity, leverage and their interaction with productivity, as well as advertising, innovation and their interactions with ICT are correlated with unobserved firm-level heterogeneity. Thus, fixed effects estimation is more appropriate for most specifications, except the innovation–ICT interaction model, where the evidence against random effects is weaker.

### 5.5.2 Breusch-Pagan Test

```{r tab-bp}

datasummary_df(
  bp_table,
  title = 'Results of Breusch-Pagan Test for Heteroscedasticity',
  output = 'kableExtra',
  escape = FALSE
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = 'HOLD_position')

```

Breusch–Pagan tests for heteroskedasticity (Table 11) strongly reject the null of constant error variance across all model specifications, indicating the presence of heteroskedasticity in the panel data. This is consistent with the underlying heterogeneity in firm characteristics such as size, industry structure and degree of global integration which can lead to high variation in GVC outcomes. However, all regressions employ two-way clustered standard errors at the firm and year level, which are robust to heteroskedasticity as well as serial correlation, ensuring robust statistical inference.

### 5.5.3 Wooldridge Autocorrelation Test

```{r tab-serialcorr}

datasummary_df(
  serialcorr_table,
  title = 'Results of Wooldridge Test for Autocorrelation',
  output = 'kableExtra',
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = 'HOLD_position')

```

Wooldridge tests for serial correlation (Table 12) indicate that the productivity specification and the capability model (advertising and innovation) suffer from significant first-order serial correlation, suggesting persistence in unobserved firm-level shocks to GVC position over time. In contrast, models incorporating financial variables (liquidity and leverage) and digital capability interactions (advertising–ICT) do not exhibit evidence of serial correlation. The innovation–ICT interaction model shows weak evidence of serial correlation at the 10% level. To account for any remaining concerns, all regressions employ two-way clustered standard errors at the firm and year level to ensure robustness.

### 5.5.4 VIF Test

```{r tab-vif}

datasummary_df(
  vif_table,
  title = 'Results of VIF Test for Multicollinearity',
  output = 'kableExtra',
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = 'HOLD_position')

```

Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) diagnostics (Table 13) indicate no evidence of multicollinearity across model specifications. The adjusted GVIF values for all variables remain well below conventional thresholds, with the maximum value not exceeding 2.4 even in models including interaction terms. Slightly higher values are observed for interaction variables, but this is expected due to their construction. Overall, the results suggest that the estimated coefficients are stable and not driven by multicollinearity among regressors.

# Chapter 6: Summary & Conclusion

\noindent\hrulefill

## 6.1 Summary

This study examined the firm-level determinants of upgrading within global value chains (GVCs) in Indian manufacturing using a novel firm-level measure of GVC position. Integrating insights from trade theory, GVC governance and the resource-based view, the analysis focused on the roles of productivity, financial constraints and firm capabilities.

The results indicate that productivity is the most robust and consistent driver of upgrading. More productive firms are able to move toward higher value-added segments of the value chain, and this effect holds both across firms and within firms over time. In contrast, the role of financial constraints is more nuanced and highly context-dependent. While leverage is found to be significant, liquidity does not exhibit a statistically significant effect. Moreover, firm fixed effects suggest that leverage primarily explains cross-sectional variation rather than within-firm upgrading, indicating that overall, financial constraints may not be associated with GVC upgrading outcomes of firms. However, both leverage and liquidity display substantial industry-level heterogeneity, suggesting that the impact of financial constraints is sector-specific and mediated by differences in production structure, capital intensity and GVC organization across industries.

Firm capabilities yield mixed results. Advertising and marketing-related expenditures emerge as significant drivers of upgrading, highlighting the importance of downstream, market-facing capabilities. However, innovation does not show a statistically significant effect, either independently or in interaction with other variables. The role of ICT is also complex: while ICT by itself is not significant, its interaction with advertising is positive and significant, suggesting that digital capabilities enhance the effectiveness of market-facing investments. At the same time, the standalone effect of advertising weakens in the presence of ICT interactions, indicating complementarity between the two.

Overall, the findings suggest that upgrading within GVCs is primarily driven by productivity and selective firm capabilities, with financial constraints and digital factors playing more context-dependent and heterogeneous roles.

## 6.2 Key Findings

- Productivity is the dominant driver of upgrading: It significantly explains both cross-sectional differences and within-firm movement along the value chain.
- Liquidity is not a binding constraint on average: Working capital does not show a statistically significant effect in the baseline results.
- Leverage matters, but primarily across firms: It explains differences in GVC position across firms but does not significantly drive within-firm upgrading when firm fixed effects are considered.
- Impact of financial constraints are highly sector-specific: The effects of both leverage and liquidity vary significantly across industries, indicating that their impact depends on sectoral characteristics such as capital intensity and GVC structure.
- Advertising drives upgrading; innovation does not: Market-facing capabilities are significant, while R&D expenditures do not show measurable effects.
- ICT has no standalone effect but acts as a complement: The interaction between ICT and advertising is positive and significant, even though ICT alone is insignificant.

## 6.3 Policy Recommendations

The empirical results collectively suggest that upgrading within global value chains is driven less by short-term financial conditions and more by deeper, capability-based factors. While productivity consistently emerges as a robust determinant of GVC positioning, financial variables such as liquidity and leverage play, at best, a limited and context-specific role. In contrast, firm-level capabilities — especially those related to marketing and digital adoption — show stronger and more nuanced effects. Further, the significance of their interaction terms highlights that capabilities do not operate in isolation; rather, it is the complementarity between digital technology and market-facing capability that enables firms to move toward higher value-added segments. At the same time, the weak and inconsistent results for innovation may reflect measurement limitations, but also point to structural constraints in translating R&D spending into functional upgrading in developing countries. Overall, the findings reinforce the idea that GVC upgrading is a gradual, capability-intensive process shaped by firm heterogeneity and industry structure.

From a policy perspective, this implies that strategies focused solely on expanding GVC participation or easing financial constraints are unlikely to drive sustained upgrading. Instead, policy should prioritize the development of firm capabilities, particularly in areas such as digital adoption, branding and market access. This includes targeted support for ICT diffusion, incentives for marketing and design capabilities and institutional mechanisms that help firms integrate into higher-value segments (e.g. export promotion agencies, cluster-based support systems). Additionally, given the heterogeneity observed across industries, a "one-size-fits-all" approach is unlikely to be effective; sector-specific policies that account for differences in production structure and technological intensity are crucial. Finally, improving the quality and effectiveness of innovation systems — ensuring that R&D leads to commercially viability — remains an important long-term objective. Taken together, our findings suggest that moving up the value chain requires not just participation, but the deliberate accumulation of complementary capabilities supported by an enabling policy environment.

## 6.4 Scope for Future Research

This study opens up several avenues for further research, particularly in refining the understanding of how firm capabilities interact with the structure of global value chains (GVCs).

A key extension would be to explicitly account for the upstream/downstream positioning of industries using the framework developed by Antras et al. (2012). Categorizing industries based on their upstream or downstream orientation would allow for a more nuanced test of capability-specific effects. In particular, future research could examine whether R&D and innovation (upstream capabilities) are more relevant for upgrading upstream, and marketing and branding (downstream capabilities) for downstream upgrading. This would help clarify the inconclusive findings on innovation in the present study and provide a more structurally grounded interpretation of capability-driven upgrading.

More broadly, the results point to the need for incorporating sector-specific production structures into empirical analyses of GVC upgrading. Future work could explore richer industry classifications based on technological intensity or governance structures to better understand the heterogeneity observed in the effects of financial constraints and firm capabilities.

Another important extension would be to improve the measurement of firm-level GVC participation. While this study relies partly on industry-level proxies for forward participation due to data limitations, future research could utilize more granular datasets, such as firm-level trade (customs) data, to construct more precise firm-level measures of value chain positioning.

Finally, future research could examine the dynamic aspects of upgrading. The current analysis focuses on contemporaneous relationships, but upgrading is inherently a gradual process involving learning and capability accumulation over time. Incorporating dynamic models could shed light on the persistence of upgrading strategies across firms.

# Appendix

## i. Software & Packages Used

All data processing and empirical analysis were conducted in R. The *tidyverse* suite was used for data cleaning and manipulation, while *prodest* was employed for the estimation of total factor productivity. Regression analysis was carried out using the *fixest* package, and model outputs and tables were generated using *modelsummary* and formatted using *kableExtra*. The *broom* package was used to tidy model outputs and extract coefficients for further analysis and visualization. Data visualization was performed using *ggplot2* and *ggrepel*. Diagnostic tests and robustness checks were conducted using the *plm* and *lmtest* packages, particularly for panel data diagnostics, along with *car* for multicollinearity analysis. Correlation analysis was supported by the *corrplot* package.

## ii. NIC-OECD Concordance Map

To construct the measure of forward participation, we map NIC industries to OECD sectors primarily at the 2-digit level via ISIC concordance (with a few exceptions at the 3–4 digit level). Since intermediate export shares from the OECD ICIO Tables are not consistently available across all industries and years, we apply a concordance based on OECD sectoral aggregation, grouping industries with similar production structures and assigning a common intermediate export share within each group. This ensures a consistent measure of forward GVC participation without arbitrarily excluding important industries.

```{r tab-concordance-chart}

datasummary_df(
  manuf_mapping,
  title = 'NIC-OECD Concordance Map',
  output = 'kableExtra',
  longtable = TRUE                                    # prints over multiple pages if required
) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = 'repeat_header') %>%  # repeats header over multiple pages
  column_spec(4:5, width = '5cm')                     # forces text (in cols 4-5) to fit in given space

```
